title: Fan-out on write: pay N inserts when posting, one lookup when reading
caption: Steps 1–4 are the publish flow (asynchronous, behind a queue); steps 5–6 are the read flow the user waits for.

steps.text: The author posts. The post service stores the body once, keyed by post id.
It publishes a 'new post' event and returns to the author right away. The fan-out happens later.
Fan-out workers pull the event and page through the author's followers in the follow graph.
They prepend the post id to every follower's timeline: 300 followers, 300 small writes, a few seconds behind the post.
A reader opens the feed. The feed service reads one key, the reader's timeline: a list of ids already in order.
It fetches the 20 post bodies in one batch read and returns the page in a few ms.

scenarios.name: Celebrity posts
scenarios.summary: A 40 M-follower account turns one post into 40 M inserts: minutes of fan-out, and every normal post queued behind it waits too.

steps.text: An account with 40 M followers posts. Storing the body and publishing the event are as cheap as ever.
The workers page through 40 M followers and start inserting, at about 100 000 inserts/s.
That's ~7 minutes before the last follower sees the post, while normal authors' events wait in the queue behind it.
Readers still get fast reads, but stale ones: their timelines are missing posts that are minutes old. This is the cue for the hybrid.

scenarios.name: Worker dies mid-way
scenarios.summary: A worker crashes halfway through the follower list. The event is redelivered and the work restarts; timelines keyed by post id make the repeated inserts harmless.

steps.text: A worker pulls the event and starts inserting the post id, batch by batch.
It crashes after some of the batches, before marking the event done.
The event was never acked, so the queue hands it to another worker, which starts again from the beginning of the follower list.
Followers that already have the post get it 'again', but a timeline is a set keyed by post id, so nothing is duplicated.

scenarios.name: Risk: inactive followers
scenarios.summary: Push writes to every follower, including the many who never come back. Skip inactive users and rebuild their timeline with pull if they return.

steps.text: A normal author posts, and the workers fetch all their followers.
Many of those followers haven't opened the app in months, yet each still gets an insert and a timeline kept in memory.
At scale that's a large share of all fan-out writes and timeline storage, spent on nobody.
Mitigation: fan out only to users active in the last ~30 days. When an inactive user returns, build their timeline once with pull, then go back to push.

scenarios.name: Alternative: hybrid
scenarios.summary: Push for normal authors, no fan-out above a follower threshold: big accounts' posts sit in a replicated cache and are merged in at read time.

steps.text: An author with a normal following posts: event to the queue, and workers push the id into each follower's timeline, as before.
An author above the threshold posts: one write, and the id goes into a hot, replicated cache of recent big-account posts. No fan-out at all.
A reader opens the feed: one timeline read, plus the recent posts of the few big accounts they follow.
Merge by time, hydrate 20 bodies, return. The cost: two code paths and a threshold to choose.
